Any field that heavily involves longterm variance and randomness whose predominate practitioners are not coming from heavy technical math backgrounds. This includes banking, investment, management, social science correlation research, soft science correlation research, and so much more. Our brains are wired extremely poorly when it comes to interpreting longterm variance. Doing so without a heavy and based mathematical foundation is little more than seeing faces in the clouds. This is made even worse by the fact that not only are we terrible at grasping variance, we're excellent at seeing patterns - even when they don't exist!

For instance, every time a "market analyst" on the news tells you why some market somewhere dropped by 0.4% yesterday - they are simply making stuff up. They take something that sounds reasonable and invent causation where none actually exists. It's like if I tell you that drowning deaths go up each year that a Nicolas Cage movie is released. That's actually true, but obviously completely unrelated. However, imagine that I told you that drowning deaths go up each year that a movie about surfing is released. Now, even though linking those two is just as unjustified without actual research indicating causation - I could say it and most people would believe me that the events are linked simply because it doesn't sound stupid, even though it is. And now I'm a market analyst.

This same sort of behavior is played out in a daily basis throughout our economic system not just by the analysts but by the people who actually have the power to make decisions. If any of this interests you (or you're interested in economics and investing in general) an awesome book on the topic is Nicholas Taleb's, "Fooled by Randomness".
